title: Enzyme-linked Receptors
terms: Cell-surface receptor whose cytosolic domain IS an enzyme or is tightly associated with one; ligand is water-soluble.
Water-soluble ligands can't cross the membrane, so the receptor faces outside (contrast steroid hormones' cytosolic receptors, LC25).
Receptor with an intrinsic guanylyl cyclase domain: guanosine triphosphate (GTP) → cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). Example: ANP receptor.
Peptide from atrial secretory granules, released by stretch (pressure/volume); lowers blood pressure. Normal ~10 pM; >100 pM pathologic.
Historically 'brain' natriuretic peptide but secreted by the VENTRICLE on distension. Normal ≤1 pM; >200 pM = badly distended heart.
Single membrane-spanning protein: extracellular binding domain, transmembrane domain, intracellular guanylyl cyclase domain. Unbound monomer = inactive.
ANP binding dimerizes the receptor; the two cyclase halves come together and become active.
Second messenger made from GTP by guanylyl cyclase; activates protein kinase G.
cGMP-activated kinase; phosphorylates CELL-TYPE/TISSUE-SPECIFIC target proteins.
PKG target in vascular smooth muscle; leads to activation of myosin light chain phosphatase.
Dephosphorylates myosin light chain → smooth muscle relaxes → vasodilation → blood pressure drops.
Terminates the signal: converts cGMP to GMP (slide typo 'PPE').
Breaks down cGMP; inhibited by sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil.
Sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), vardenafil (Levitra): erectile dysfunction, PULMONARY ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION, prostatic hyperplasia.
Protease that cleaves the 126-amino-acid natriuretic prohormone to the 28-amino-acid active peptide.
ANP/BNP receptors (slide 'NP-A/B'); mainly adrenal gland, kidney, vascular smooth muscle; → cGMP → PKG.
In adrenal cells, cGMP ↑ PDE2 → breaks down cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) → ↓ACTH-stimulated cortisol (and modestly ↓aldosterone).
Raises cAMP in adrenal cortisol-secreting cells → cortisol; ANP opposes this via PDE2.
↓Renal perfusion → renin → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II → aldosterone, vasoconstriction, ADH, sympathetic activity → ↑blood pressure.
On pulmonary and renal endothelium; converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II receptor in adrenal cortex, arterioles, pituitary; a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
ADH from posterior pituitary; V2 receptor in kidney = Gs-coupled GPCR → collecting duct water absorption. ANP ↓ADH.
Epithelial sodium channel and renal outer medullary potassium channel; aldosterone ↑ their expression in distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.
Afferent dilation → ↑GFR; ↓renin → ↓angiotensin II → ↓aldosterone; ↓ADH; vasodilation → ↓Na⁺/water retention → ↓blood pressure.
Rises when ANP dilates the afferent arteriole without changing the efferent arteriole.
Receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase; ligand brings two halves together → autophosphorylation. Mostly growth factor receptors.
The receptor's own tyrosine kinase phosphorylates its own tyrosines after ligand binding.
FGF, VEGF, NGF, IGF-1, EGF, PDGF receptors (S8): ↑proliferation, ↑cell longevity, ↓programmed cell death.
Two extracellular (binding) + two membrane-spanning (cytosolic tyrosine kinase) subunits; signals via TWO arms (IRS-1 and MAPK).
Adapter/scaffolding protein; binds activated insulin receptor and activates PI3K (skeletal muscle, adipose).
Phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3; through a series of steps drives GLUT4 vesicle fusion with the membrane.
Condensed steps between PI3K and GLUT4 insertion; Schultz: 'I don't think you need to know all those steps.'
Insulin-regulated glucose transporter stored in vesicles; inserted into the membrane → facilitated diffusion of glucose.
Constitutive glucose transporter; also a transcription target of the insulin MAPK arm.
Glucose transporter of the pancreatic β cell; lets glucose in to raise ATP:ADP.
Slide: 'adapter protein'; Schultz: GTP EXCHANGE FACTOR that swaps GDP for GTP on RAS.
MONOMERIC G protein/GTPase: GTP-bound = on, GDP-bound = off; its GTPase is the timer.
RAS = single subunit in RTK pathways; heterotrimeric (α, β, γ) = GPCR pathways (LC27).
MAPKKK (Raf) → MAPKK (MEK) → MAPK (ERK); each phosphorylates the next.
Mito = thread (chromosome in division) + gen = generate → drives cell proliferation.
The ONLY kinase in the cascade that translocates into the nucleus; activates early-gene transcription.
Transcribed after MAPK enters the nucleus; jun and fos proteins co-activate target genes (GLUT4, GLUT1, cyclin D).
Normal growth-signaling gene; mutated RAS lacking GTPase stays on → excessive proliferation → cancer. 'Your first example.'
Glucose via GLUT2 → ↑ATP:ADP → ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel closes → depolarization → insulin secretion.
Liver, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, fibrocytes (GLUT4 drawn).
Defective β cells → insufficient secretion, LOW insulin; treated with insulin.
Defective receptor/signaling in peripheral tissues; NORMAL or HIGH insulin; still treated with insulin (fewest side effects).
5 mM glucose = 90 mg/dL ('just an FYI', systems link).
Cells starve despite hyperglycemia: weight loss, polydipsia/polyuria, weakness; hyperlipidemia, ketonuria, uremia.
Glucose above renal threshold → glucosuria drags water → polyuria.
Fatty acids → acetyl-CoA → acetoacetate → 4-OH butyrate + acetone → ketoacidosis → acidotic coma; ketonuria.
Amino acid metabolism for energy → urea production → uremia.
NO intrinsic kinase; after ligand-induced dimerization recruits a non-receptor tyrosine kinase (JAK2).
Made mainly by kidney; ↑ when oxygen partial pressure (PO2) is low; ↑ erythroid progenitor proliferation in bone marrow.
Non-receptor tyrosine kinase; binds dimerized EPO receptor, phosphorylates ITSELF and the RECEPTOR. Janus = god of doorways.
Signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (STAT5)
Phosphorylated by receptor/JAK2 complex → nucleus → transcription of bcl-2.
Longevity gene: prevents apoptosis, promotes survival (EPO's JAK-STAT arm).
Secondary gene from EPO's MAPK arm (via jun/fos); needed for cell division → proliferation.
JAK inhibitor used for canine atopic dermatitis ('totally off target' side note).
Replaces EPO when a failing kidney can't make enough; misused as a doping agent.
Separates native vs recombinant EPO by charge (gel pH ~3.8–5.2); basis of rhEPO urine test.
Signals by REMOVING phosphates; example CD45 ('that's all I'm going to say').
TGF-β, bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), Müllerian inhibiting substance → SMAD; FK506 link to immunosuppression; not covered.
traps: cGMP vs cAMP: ANP → guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → protein kinase G. ACTH → cAMP → cortisol. Don't swap the letters.
PDE5 vs PDE2: PDE5 breaks down cGMP (Viagra target). PDE2 is activated by cGMP and breaks down cAMP (how ANP ↓cortisol).
ANP = atria (modest stretch, physiologic) vs BNP = ventricle (distension, pathologic). 'B' was historically 'brain' but it is NOT secreted by brain.
Units: pM for natriuretic peptides (ANP 10 pM normal, >100 pM pathologic; BNP ≤1 pM, >200 pM bad) vs mM for glucose. Watch pM vs nM vs mM options.
Autophosphorylation (receptor tyrosine kinase: insulin, growth factors) vs JAK2 phosphorylates the receptor (EPO receptor has NO intrinsic kinase).
MAPKKK → MAPKK → MAPK: each K phosphorylates the next; only MAPK enters the nucleus. RAS activates MAPKKK (Schultz's correction), it doesn't phosphorylate it.
RAS-GTP = ON, RAS-GDP = OFF. SOS loads GTP; RAS's own GTPase turns it off. Mutant RAS without GTPase = always on → tumor (proto-oncogene).
Insulin's two arms: IRS-1 → PI3K = insert GLUT4 now; SOS → RAS → MAPK = transcribe GLUT4 for next time.
EPO's two arms: STAT5 → bcl-2 = survival (↓apoptosis); MAPK → cyclin D = proliferation. Don't swap the products.
GLUT2 = β-cell glucose sensor; GLUT4 = insulin-regulated target-tissue transporter. IDD = low insulin, IRD = normal/high insulin, BOTH treated with insulin.
Corin cleaves pro-ANP (126 → 28 amino acids) vs renin cleaves angiotensinogen. ANP ↓ renin, aldosterone, ADH; ANP ↑ GFR.

quiz.stem: Binding of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) to its receptor directly activates which enzyme activity? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Guanylyl cyclase activity of the receptor itself
bad: Adenylyl cyclase activity of an associated Gs protein
Tyrosine kinase activity of the receptor itself
Phospholipase C activity of an associated Gq protein
Janus kinase activity recruited to the receptor
quiz.why: The ANP receptor has an intrinsic intracellular guanylyl cyclase domain: GTP → cGMP. (Asked on Quiz07.)

quiz.stem: A dog's plasma atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is measured at 150 pM. Using Dr. Schultz's cutoffs, how is this interpreted? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Pathologic; above the 100 pM ANP cutoff
bad: Healthy; well below the 100 nM ANP cutoff
Healthy; near the 10 pM ANP normal
Healthy; below the 200 pM BNP cutoff
Pathologic; above the 1 pM ANP normal
quiz.why: ANP ~10 pM is healthy; >100 pM is pathologic. 100 nM is a unit trap; 200 pM is the BNP number; 1 pM is BNP's normal.

quiz.stem: A cat's plasma B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 250 pM. Which interpretation fits the lecture? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Badly distended ventricle; BNP is secreted by the ventricle
bad: Badly distended atria; BNP is secreted by the atrial wall
Normal value; BNP is normally near 250 pM in plasma
Brain injury; BNP is secreted by brain neurons
Normal value; BNP is normally near 250 nM in plasma
quiz.why: BNP is historically 'brain' but comes from the ventricle; normal ≤1 pM; >200 pM = badly distended heart. (BNP source asked on Quiz07.)

quiz.stem: Sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil inhibit phosphodiesterase 5. Besides erectile dysfunction, which clinical use did Dr. Schultz name? (select one correct response)
bad: Systemic arterial hypotension in shock
Canine atopic dermatitis
Insulin-resistant diabetes
Chronic renal anemia
quiz.why: PDE5 inhibitors keep cGMP high (vasodilation); used for erectile dysfunction, pulmonary arterial hypertension, prostatic hyperplasia.

quiz.stem: In adrenal cortisol-secreting cells, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) raises cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). How does atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) reduce ACTH-stimulated cortisol secretion? (select one correct response)
bad: ↑cGMP activates phosphodiesterase 5, which degrades cAMP
↑cAMP activates phosphodiesterase 2, which degrades cGMP
↑cGMP activates protein kinase G, which blocks ACTH binding
↓cGMP inactivates phosphodiesterase 2, which preserves cAMP
quiz.why: ANP → cGMP → ↑PDE2 activity → cAMP broken down → ↓cortisol (same mechanism modestly ↓aldosterone). (Asked on Quiz07.)

quiz.stem: Natriuretic peptides are released from the heart as a 126-amino-acid prohormone. Which enzyme activates it, and what is the active peptide's length? (select one correct response)
bad: Renin; 28-amino-acid active peptide
Corin; 126-amino-acid active peptide
Angiotensin-converting enzyme; 28-amino-acid peptide
Corin; 128-amino-acid active peptide
quiz.why: Corin cleaves the 126-aa prohormone to the 28-aa active form (Schultz corrected himself from 128 to 126).

quiz.stem: Which effects result from activation of natriuretic peptide receptors A/B (NPR-A/B)? (select all that apply)
bad: Increased antidiuretic hormone secretion
Arteriolar smooth muscle contraction
quiz.why: Afferent dilation ↑GFR; kidney vasodilation ↓renin → ↓angiotensin II → ↓aldosterone; pituitary NP receptors ↓ADH; vessels dilate.

quiz.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) dilates the afferent arteriole while the efferent arteriole is unchanged. What happens to glomerular filtration rate (GFR)? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Increases, putting more fluid into the nephron
bad: Decreases, putting less fluid into the nephron
Increases, because the efferent arteriole dilates
Decreases, because renin secretion is stimulated
Unchanged, because both arterioles stay matched
quiz.why: Afferent dilation without efferent change → ↑GFR → more fluid delivered to the nephron.

quiz.stem: Fibroblast growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, and nerve growth factor receptors share which activation step? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Ligand brings halves together; tyrosines autophosphorylate
bad: Ligand brings halves together; Janus kinase 2 is recruited
Ligand brings halves together; cyclic GMP is generated
Ligand releases a heterotrimeric G protein from the receptor
Ligand brings halves together; CD45 removes phosphates
quiz.why: Receptor tyrosine kinases: agonist → two halves together → intrinsic tyrosine kinase → autophosphorylation.

quiz.stem: In skeletal muscle, the insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS-1) adapter protein directly activates which enzyme? (select one correct response)
bad: Mitogen-activated protein kinase
Janus kinase 2
Protein kinase G
Myosin light chain phosphatase
quiz.why: Activated insulin receptor → IRS-1 → PI3K (PIP2 → PIP3) → GLUT4 vesicle fusion. (Asked on Quiz07.)

quiz.stem: Which steps lie between insulin binding and GLUT4 insertion through the IRS-1 arm? (select all that apply)
ok: Autophosphorylation of receptor tyrosine kinase domains
Association of the receptor with IRS-1
bad: Exchange of GDP for GTP on RAS by SOS
Translocation of MAPK into the nucleus
quiz.why: IRS-1 arm: autophosphorylation → IRS-1 → PI3K → GLUT4 vesicle fusion. SOS/RAS/MAPK belong to the second arm (GLUT4 synthesis).

quiz.stem: Per Dr. Schultz's in-class correction, how does RAS-GTP act on MAP kinase kinase kinase (Raf)? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Activates it by direct interaction, not phosphorylation
bad: Phosphorylates it on a tyrosine residue to fully activate it
Phosphorylates it on a serine residue to activate it
Dephosphorylates it to remove an inhibitory phosphate
Hydrolyzes its own GTP to transfer phosphate to it
quiz.why: Slides (S10, S12) show 'phosphorylation of MAPKKK'; Schultz said a newer review shows RAS activates it by interaction. See flag.

quiz.stem: In the insulin receptor's mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) arm, which kinase translocates into the nucleus? (select one correct response)
bad: MAP kinase kinase (MEK)
MAP kinase kinase kinase (Raf)
Phosphoinositide 3-kinase
Janus kinase 2
quiz.why: Only phosphorylated MAPK translocates into the nucleus and activates early genes (myc, jun, fos). (Trap asked on Quiz07.)

quiz.stem: A RAS mutation abolishes its intrinsic GTPase activity, but son of sevenless (SOS) still functions. Which state does RAS stay in? (select one correct response)
bad: GDP-bound and switched off
GTP-bound and switched off
GDP-bound and switched on
Nucleotide-free and switched off
quiz.why: SOS loads GTP; without GTPase RAS can't hydrolyze GTP → stays on. GTPase is the timer.

quiz.stem: Continuing the previous question (RAS lacking GTPase activity), what outcome does the lecture predict? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Excessive proliferation; RAS acts as a proto-oncogene
bad: Excessive apoptosis; RAS acts as a tumor suppressor
Reduced proliferation; MAPK signaling is terminated
Excessive proliferation; JAK2 is always switched on
Reduced survival; bcl-2 transcription is blocked
quiz.why: MAPK pathway always on → mitogenesis → tumors. 'Your first example of a proto-oncogene.'

quiz.stem: In a pancreatic β cell, glucose enters via GLUT2 and raises the ATP:ADP ratio. What happens next? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close, depolarizing the cell
bad: ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels open, hyperpolarizing the cell
ATP-sensitive Ca²⁺ channels close, hyperpolarizing the cell
GLUT4 vesicles fuse with membrane, depolarizing the cell
Insulin receptors autophosphorylate, depolarizing the cell
quiz.why: ↑ATP:ADP ↓K⁺ channel activity → depolarization → insulin secretion.

quiz.stem: A cat's resting plasma glucose is 30 mM. Using 5 mM = 90 mg/dL, what is the value in mg/dL and its S16 category? (select one correct response)
bad: 540 mg/dL; in the after-dinner range
167 mg/dL; in the diabetes range
54 mg/dL; in the normal resting range
270 mg/dL; in the after-dinner range
quiz.why: 30 mM × 18 = 540 mg/dL. 30 mM falls in 22–44 mM = diabetes (after-dinner is 14–17 mM).

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly describes the erythropoietin (EPO) receptor? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: No intrinsic kinase; recruits Janus kinase 2 after dimerization
bad: Intrinsic tyrosine kinase; autophosphorylates after dimerization
No intrinsic kinase; generates cGMP itself after dimerization
Intrinsic guanylyl cyclase; makes cGMP after it dimerizes
No intrinsic kinase; recruits IRS-1 and PI3K after dimerization
quiz.why: Tyrosine-kinase-associated receptor: cytosolic domain lacks kinase activity; EPO → dimerization → JAK2 binds. (EPO → JAK asked on Quiz07.)

quiz.stem: Ferbitinib, an invented drug, selectively blocks MAP kinase kinase (MEK). In an erythroid progenitor stimulated by erythropoietin (EPO), which response is most directly reduced? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Cyclin D transcription via the MAPK arm
bad: Bcl-2 transcription via the STAT5 arm
JAK2 autophosphorylation at the receptor
STAT5 phosphorylation by the JAK2 complex
GDP-to-GTP exchange on RAS by SOS
quiz.why: MEK sits downstream of SOS/RAS and upstream of MAPK → cyclin D. The JAK2/STAT5 → bcl-2 arm is untouched.

quiz.stem: Which events are part of erythropoietin (EPO) receptor signaling? (select all that apply)
ok: JAK2 phosphorylates itself and the receptor
Phosphorylated STAT5 moves into the nucleus
Transcription of the survival gene bcl-2
Transcription of the cell-cycle gene cyclin D
bad: Receptor tyrosine kinase domain autophosphorylates
quiz.why: EPO receptor has no intrinsic kinase; JAK2 does the phosphorylating. Arms: STAT5 → bcl-2 and SOS/RAS/MAPK → cyclin D.

flags: S4 typo: 'PPE'
S4 says 'Phosphodiesterase (PPE) converts cGMP to GMP'; Schultz: typo, should be phosphodiesterase (PDE) · use PDE.
MAPKKK phosphorylated vs activated (S10, S12, S19)

Slides/figures: 'phosphorylation of MAPKKK' by RAS-GTP; Schultz (newer review): RAS ACTIVATES MAPKKK by interaction, not phosphorylation · use Schultz's correction; MAPKKK → MAPKK → MAPK are phosphorylations.
ANP vs RAAS side-by-side slide not in posted deck

Transcript describes a slide with RAAS on the right and ANP on the left (corin, 126 → 28 amino acids, PDE2/cortisol, NPR-A/B, ↓ADH); posted S5 shows RAAS only, S6–S7 cover ANP generally · those facts cited 'transcript'; ask for the updated slide.
'NRR-A' label typo
In-class slide said 'NRR-A'; Schultz: natriuretic peptide receptor A or B. Posted S7 says 'NP-A/B' · use NPR-A/B.
S2 lists RAS under receptor tyrosine kinases
RAS is not a receptor; Schultz: a monomeric G protein that is part of the RTK pathway (S13) · treat RAS as a pathway component.
SOS: 'adapter protein' (S12, S19) vs 'exchange factor' (transcript)
Slides call SOS an adapter; Schultz calls it a GTP exchange factor that swaps GDP for GTP on RAS · know both. OUTSIDE—confirm: SOS is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor; Grb2 is the adapter.
Apoquel (oclacitinib) JAK target
Schultz first said 'JAK-4', then 'JAK1 and 3' (unsure). OUTSIDE—confirm: oclacitinib is JAK1-preferential · for now just 'JAK inhibitor for canine atopic dermatitis'; don't commit to a number.
Renin trigger: 'distention' (transcript) vs ↓renal perfusion (S5)
Transcript: 'distention at the juxtaglomerular apparatus' releases renin; S5: 'decrease in renal perfusion' · slides win (likely misspeak/garble).
'Corticotropes' in the adrenal gland

Schultz calls adrenal cortisol-secreting cells 'corticotropes'. OUTSIDE—confirm: corticotropes usually = anterior pituitary ACTH cells; adrenal cortisol cells = zona fasciculata · know the mechanism, not the cell name.
S14 lists liver among GLUT4 target tissues
S14 draws GLUT4 on liver, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, fibrocytes; S11 says skeletal muscle and adipose. OUTSIDE—confirm: hepatocytes mainly use GLUT2 · slide wins for exam.
S16 '4-OH butyrate'
OUTSIDE—confirm: standard name is β-hydroxybutyrate (3-hydroxybutyrate) · use the slide's chain on the exam.
Proto-oncogene wording (S13)
S13: 'RAS is called a proto-oncogene.' OUTSIDE—confirm: normal RAS gene = proto-oncogene; GTPase-dead mutant = oncogene · use slide wording.
ANP vs BNP prohormone size
Schultz: ANP or BNP released as 126-amino-acid prohormone → 28-amino-acid active peptide. OUTSIDE—confirm: those numbers are ANP's; BNP differs · use 126 → 28 for ANP.
PI3K name (S11)
S11: 'phospho-inositol-3-kinase'. OUTSIDE: standard name phosphoinositide 3-kinase · same enzyme.
S4 asterisks without footnote
S4 marks 'monomer*' and 'dimerization*' with no footnote; transcript confirms ANP binding → dimerization → active cyclase · nothing to resolve unless a footnote appears.
S8 'Epithelial Growth Factor Receptor'
S8 labels EGF receptor 'Epithelial'. OUTSIDE—confirm: standard name is epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor · same receptor; either name should be accepted.
Janus 'Greek god'
Schultz: Janus = Greek god of doorways. OUTSIDE: Janus is a Roman god · not testable.
